title: Who Gets a Seat at the Table
overview: At a dinner on the Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, Jesus heals a sick man, challenges how people chase status and choose their guests, tells a story about a feast filled with outsiders, and then warns the crowds about the cost of following him.

parts.label: Healing at a Sabbath dinner (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: Work was forbidden on the Sabbath, and teachers argued over whether healing counted as work, so the religious leaders at this dinner watched closely as Jesus faced a man badly swollen with fluid. He heals him, then asks whether they would not pull their own ox out of a well that same day, and they have no answer.

parts.label: Where to sit at the table (vv. 7-11)
parts.note: Seats at a meal were ranked by honor, and guests were jostling for the best ones, so Jesus echoes an old proverb (Proverbs 25:6-7): take the lowest seat and let the host move you up. The closing line shows he means more than good manners, because God reverses who is honored.

parts.label: Who to invite (vv. 12-14)
parts.note: A dinner invitation usually came with the expectation of being invited back. Jesus tells his host to invite people who could never return the favor, and says the reward will come when the righteous are raised from the dead.

parts.label: The great banquet (vv. 15-24)
parts.note: A guest mentions the feast in God's kingdom, an old Jewish picture of the age to come, and Jesus answers with a story in which the invited guests offer polite excuses, so the host fills his house first with the poor and disabled of the town and then with people from the roads outside it. A common reading is that respected insiders turn down Jesus's invitation while outcasts, and later non-Jews, accept it, and the order to press people to come in is often taken as urging those who feel unworthy.

parts.label: The cost of following (vv. 25-33)
parts.note: Carrying a cross meant walking to your own execution, and many read "hate" here as a Hebrew way of saying "love less by comparison," though how far these demands about family and possessions go is debated. The half-built tower and the outnumbered king make the same point: count the cost before you begin.

parts.label: Salt that goes flat (vv. 34-35)
parts.note: Salt that has lost its taste is useless, not even good for a field or a manure pile, and is thrown away. Exactly how salt lost its taste in that world is unclear, but the picture is of a follower whose commitment has gone flat.

disagreement: Christians differ over whether Jesus's call to put him above family and to part with all one has is meant literally, as some monastic traditions practice, or as a call to put him first while still living an ordinary life with family and possessions.
think: Have you ever been welcomed by someone who expected nothing in return, and how did it change the way you saw them or yourself?
